items.stem: What does Siddhartha see moving through the high forest canopy?
items.quote: Siddhartha saw a group of apes moving through the high canopy of the forest
items.why: He now notices the living world around him.

items.stem: What is the young woman at the stream doing when Siddhartha arrives?
items.quote: a young woman was kneeling and washing clothes
items.why: The village scene is his first meeting on the road to the city.

items.stem: Where had Siddhartha slept the night before he reached the city?
items.quote: the straw hut of the ferryman, in which he had slept that night
items.why: It was the first roof over his head in a long time.

items.stem: Whom does Siddhartha make friends with that first evening in the city?
items.quote: he made friends with barber’s assistant
items.why: An ordinary friendship marks his first evening among city people.

items.stem: Kamala claps her hands after hearing Siddhartha's poem.
items.quote: Kamala loudly clapped her hands, so that the golden bracelets clanged.
items.why: Her clapping shows the poem pleased her.

items.stem: At the inn, Siddhartha eats the rice cake he is given.
items.quote: He gave the rice cake to a dog and remained without food.
items.why: He accepts the cake but does not eat it.

items.stem: Complete: “Kamala smiled, played with her fan of ____ feathers”
items.quote: Kamala smiled, played with her fan of peacocks’ feathers
items.why: Small luxuries mark Kamala's world.

items.stem: Complete: the lady sat “on red ____ under a colourful canopy”
items.quote: on red pillows under a colourful canopy
items.why: The detail shows Kamala's wealth.

he saw the pike hungrily hunting for its dinner

he reached the large city before the evening

items.stem: How does Siddhartha say he addresses Kamala, unlike other women?
items.quote: You are the first woman whom Siddhartha is not addressing with his eyes turned to the ground.
items.why: He meets her gaze directly.

items.stem: Besides thinking, waiting and fasting, what does Siddhartha say he can also do?
items.quote: But yes, I can also write poetry.
items.why: He names one more skill.

items.stem: What gift does the maid hand Siddhartha as she leads him out?
items.quote: being given upper garments as a gift
items.why: Kamala quietly equips him for the city.

items.stem: How does Siddhartha feel after Kamala's first kiss?
items.quote: was in this moment astonished like a child
items.why: Her kiss opens a whole new field of learning to him.

items.stem: Siddhartha gets out of the grove and over the hedge without a sound.
items.quote: he managed to get out of the grove and over the hedge without making a sound.
items.why: His forest habits help him leave unseen.

items.stem: When Siddhartha greets her at the grove, Kamala frowns and hurries past.
items.quote: With a smile, the beautiful women nodded for a moment and disappeared into the grove
items.why: She smiles and nods before she disappears.

items.stem: Complete the poem: “At the grove’s entrance stood the brown ____.”
items.quote: At the grove’s entrance stood the brown Samana.
items.why: His poem tells their first meeting.

items.stem: Match each person to their action during the visit.
items.why: Each reaction shapes the first visit.
evidence: At this, Kamala laughed aloud.
Siddhartha bowed with a smile.
Siddhartha found himself being dragged away by the maid

items.stem: Put these moments of the first visit in order.
items.why: The visit runs from greeting to sudden interruption.

Siddhartha spoke, after he had thought about it for a moment, these verses:

a maid came running in

items.why: He leaves in secret and returns the next day.

cards.text: He gives a dog his rice cake
He is told to hurry away

evidence: “Hurry and get yourself away, Siddhartha, nobody may see you in here, remember that!
over the hedge without making a sound.

there he turned up the following day.

items.stem: Why is Siddhartha happy to reach the city that evening?
items.quote: was happy, for he felt the need to be among people.
items.why: After years in the forest, he longs for human company.

items.stem: Why does Kamala say verses alone will not be enough for him?
items.quote: But it will be difficult for you to earn thus much money with verses as you need.
items.why: Being Kamala's friend has a price.

items.stem: Why must Siddhartha hurry out of Kamala's house?
items.quote: “There’s a visitor for me,”
items.why: No one may see him there.

items.stem: Why does Kamala tell him not to be too modest with Kamaswami?
items.quote: I do not want you to become his servant, you shall become his equal
items.why: Kamala aims high for him.

items.stem: Siddhartha tells Kamala there are no daemons behind what fools call magic.
items.quote: Nothing is effected by daemons, there are no daemons.
items.why: He credits patient will, not spirits.

items.stem: Siddhartha says he still wants to sing the sacrificial songs.
items.quote: but I do not want to sing them any more.
items.why: He sets his old priestly skills aside.

items.stem: Learning he had not eaten, Kamala “sent for bread and ____”
items.quote: she sent for bread and fruits and treated him to it.
items.why: Her care follows from learning he went hungry.

items.stem: Siddhartha thinks: “I will not be able to enter the ____ like this.”
items.quote: I must not remain like this, I will not be able to enter the grove like this.
items.why: This thought drives him to change before visiting her.

items.stem: Match each cause to its effect.
items.why: Each moment of the visit has a clear result.
evidence: “There’s a visitor for me,”
she sent for bread and fruits
truly, I’m losing nothing when I give you a kiss for them.

items.stem: Order these steps in Siddhartha's change.
items.why: He moves from forest seeker toward city life.

cards.text: He earns a kiss with a poem
He vows never to lower his eyes
He says he knew she'd help

evidence: Never again I want to turn my eyes to the ground
I’m losing nothing when I give you a kiss for them.

items.stem: Kamala's mouth is “like a freshly cracked fig.” What does the simile chiefly suggest?
items.quote: a bright red mouth like a freshly cracked fig
items.why: The fruit image makes her beauty vivid and inviting.

items.stem: “every hour sped swiftly away like a sail on the sea, and under the sail was a ship full of treasures” suggests what about his days?
items.quote: every hour sped swiftly away like a sail on the sea, and under the sail was a ship full of treasures, full of joy.
items.why: Each passing hour now carries delight.

items.stem: He had tried “to capture it in the net of thought.” The image suggests what about finding the self?
items.quote: But he had never really found this self, because he had wanted to capture it in the net of thought.
items.why: The self slips through any net of ideas.

items.stem: Which phrase best shows he now trusts an inner voice over outside rules?
items.quote: To obey like this, not to an external command, only to the voice
items.why: He chooses inner guidance over teachers and rules.

items.stem: “Never again I want to turn my eyes to the ground” chiefly marks what change?
items.quote: Never again I want to turn my eyes to the ground, when I’m coming across a beautiful woman.
items.why: The ascetic who looked away now looks at life.

items.stem: Calling the world of before “a fleeting, deceptive veil” shows how differently Siddhartha now sees it.
items.quote: nothing more to Siddhartha than a fleeting, deceptive veil
items.why: What he once dismissed he now finds beautiful.

items.stem: Siddhartha credits his coming success entirely to Kamala's help.
items.quote: when I came to you into your grove, I did the first step.
items.why: He insists he took the first step himself.

items.stem: Complete his farewell wish: “that always good ____ shall come to me out of your direction!”
items.quote: that always good fortune shall come to me out of your direction!
items.why: He leaves wishing for luck from her.

items.why: Phrases reveal speakers' attitudes.
